articleTitle: A low cost PC based nuclear spectrometer
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Modern Methods of Detecting and Measuring Ionising Radiations
abstract: Describes the development of a gamma radiation spectrometer based upon a personal computer. The current spectrometer market for both hardware instruments and their PC centred alternatives is in the main an expensive one. In addition to expense, many systems are not particularly versatile and incorporate inflexible software. In many cases, where a computer forms the system hub, additional instrumentation is required to produce a complete spectrometer. Some systems have to be specified ab initio and are not user reconfigurable. A gap was identified for an alternative to the above products which would be significantly cheaper yet still retain the performance required. Equally it was considered vitally important to introduce a significant degree of flexibility and user friendliness. It was not intended that any other additional instrumentation beyond the PC enclosure would be necessary.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Instrumentation in the ionising radiation field
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Modern Methods of Detecting and Measuring Ionising Radiations
abstract: The author describes elementary operational details of: (i) proportional counters; (ii) ionisation chambers; and (iii) Geiger counters. Comparisons are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Modern Methods of Detecting and Measuring Ionising Radiations
abstract: In a number of applications in ionising radiation dosimetry, new technologies can be of considerable benefit. This work describes a new type of direct-reading semiconductor dosimeter which has been studied in laboratories for a number of years but has hitherto not been used in large numbers in the field. The examples of applications described serves to show how this new technology has left the laboratory and is quickly gaining acceptance in the field.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Modern Methods of Detecting and Measuring Ionising Radiations
abstract: Although there have been only very small advances in recent years in radiation detectors such as Geiger counters, scintillation counters, semiconductor detectors, etc., this doesn't mean that there has not been dramatic advances in radiation protection instrumentation. This has been due to the far greater use of microprocessors to manipulate the limited amount of information provided by detectors. This use of processors is spreading throughout the industry and there are few radiation protection instruments under development which do not incorporate microprocessors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Radiometric instrumentation at the Sellafield reprocessing complex
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Modern Methods of Detecting and Measuring Ionising Radiations
abstract: The safe handling and routing of radioactive materials in an operational reprocessing facility requires the provision of monitoring instrumentation capable of detecting and quantifying the activities of specific radioisotopes and/or fissile contents. Such instrumentation is required for a number of purposes: safeguards to ensure that the 'nuclear material' inventory of the plant is properly accounted for; quality checking of used fuel fed to the reprocessing plant, to ensure conformation to the envelope of allowable initial enrichment, irradiation and cooling time; process and criticality control during all phases of the reprocessing operations; and ensuring that both product and waste streams comply with the appropriate transport and storage/disposal regulations. BNFL have developed many such monitoring instruments, for situations where no commercial systems are available, the emphasis being on the cost effective achievement of accurate and reliable measurement. This work describes some of the radiometric techniques which have been utilised in such instrumentation. A number of examples are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Modern Methods of Detecting and Measuring Ionising Radiations
abstract: Most of the radon measurement techniques used to date rely heavily on methods developed for laboratory use or for underground mining applications. This work describes a generation of new, electronic devices which have been developed to measure radon on site. Applications include measurements in homes, offices and underground sites.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Measurement techniques used in the development of environmental radioactivity standards at the National Physical Laboratory
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Modern Methods of Detecting and Measuring Ionising Radiations
abstract: NPL's Division of Radiation Science and Acoustics (DRSA) provides standards and calibration services in the fields of ionizing radiation and radioactivity, acoustics, and ultrasonics. Radioactivity standards are provided by the Radioactivity Group, which has the following functions: (1) to develop and maintain the UK primary standards for radionuclide metrology; (2) to disseminate the standards through calibration and measurement services, secondary standards and reference data; (3) to promulgate good measurement practices and provide information, advice and training courses on measurement techniques; (4) to collaborate with European and international organisations to further the development and adoption of new measurement techniques and harmonised measurement protocols. In recent years, environmental radioactivity monitoring laboratories have come under increasing pressure to demonstrate that their measurements are traceable to national standards; this has led to a demand for standards and calibration services at the environmental level. The required standards can be categorised as follows: (1) single and mixed nuclide solutions; (2) spiked reference materials (SRMs); (3) gas standards. NPL has responded to these requirements by expanding its metrological capacity in the radioactivity field to accommodate low-level measurements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Radiometric instrumentation for plant environmental monitoring at BNFL Sellafield
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Modern Methods of Detecting and Measuring Ionising Radiations
abstract: BNFL has detailed experience and knowledge in the application of installed radiometric instrumentation, primarily at Sellafield. The range of applications is extensive and comprises: (i) process monitoring; (ii) waste characterisation; (iii) fissile material accountancy; (iv) environmental discharge monitoring; (v) workplace monitoring. The scale of the systems ranges from single stand alone instruments to large building surveillance and evacuation systems incorporating many airborne contamination monitors. Over 600 alpha-in-air monitors, 1000beta-in-air monitors and 500gamma monitors have been installed in 30 new plants at Sellafield since 1975.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
